modern_osis:
Original chapter heading

What animals were clean and unclean.

Clean and unclean animals

Henry sees several purposes behind the laws distinguishing clean and unclean animals.

First, they tested Israel's obedience, just as Adam's refusal to eat from the tree of knowledge was a test.

They also taught self-denial and control over bodily appetite.

Second, they kept Israel distinct from other nations.

Many of the forbidden animals were objects of pagan superstition or idolatry.

Third, the laws taught the people to distinguish between the holy and the unholy when choosing companions and close relationships.

Fourth, the law prohibited not only eating unclean animals but also touching them.

Those who wish to avoid sin must also be careful to avoid its temptations and circumstances that draw them close to it.

The regulations contained very detailed exceptions.

Those details required continuous attentiveness and precise obedience, training the people to obey God's commands.

Christians are now free from these burdensome ceremonial rules.

Yet we must not misuse our freedom.

The Lord has redeemed and called his people to be holy as he is holy.

We must turn away from the sinful patterns of the world and avoid unnecessary close ties with those who remain spiritually dead.

We should be eager to do good, devoted to God and glad to keep company with his people.
classic_reading:
[Lev.11.1]
Chapter 11
What animals were clean and unclean.
--These laws seem to have been intended, 1. As a test of the people's obedience, as Adam was forbidden to eat of the tree of knowledge; and to teach them self-denial, and the government of their appetites. 2. To keep the Israelites distinct from other nations. Many also of these forbidden animals were objects of superstition and idolatry to the heathen. 3. The people were taught to make distinctions between the holy and unholy in their companions and intimate connexions. 4. The law forbad, not only the eating of the unclean beasts, but the touching of them. Those who would be kept from any sin, must be careful to avoid all temptations to it, or coming near it. The exceptions are very minute, and all were designed to call forth constant care and exactness in their obedience; and to teach us to obey. Whilst we enjoy our Christian liberty, and are free from such burdensome observances, we must be careful not to abuse our liberty. For the Lord hath redeemed and called his people, that they may be holy, even as he is holy. We must come out, and be separate from the world; we must leave the company of the ungodly, and all needless connexions with those who are dead in sin; we must be zealous of good works devoted followers of God, and companions of his people.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Ceremonial purification.

Purification after childbirth

After the laws concerning clean and unclean food come laws concerning people who were considered ceremonially clean or unclean.

Henry understands these regulations in light of the fallen condition inherited by every child.

Human beings pass their corrupt nature on to their descendants.

Apart from the atonement of Christ and the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit, even the original blessing to increase and multiply (Genesis 1:28) has become bound up with the transmission of sin and misery throughout the fallen human family.

Women who have received God's mercy in childbirth should respond with heartfelt gratitude for his goodness.

Such thanksgiving pleases him more than sacrifices.
classic_reading:
[Lev.12.1]
Chapter 12
Ceremonial purification.
--After the laws concerning clean and unclean food, come the laws concerning clean and unclean persons. Man imparts his depraved nature to his offspring, so that, excepting as the atonement of Christ and the sanctification of the Spirit prevent, the original blessing, "Increase and multiply," [Gen.1.28] Ge 1:28, is become to the fallen race a direful curse, and communicates sin and misery. Let those women who have received mercy from God in child-bearing, with all thankfulness own God's goodness to them; and this shall please the Lord better than sacrifices.

The priest examines suspected skin disease (verses 1–17)

The affliction called leprosy was treated primarily as a condition of ceremonial uncleanness rather than an ordinary illness.

Henry notes that Christ is said to cleanse those afflicted, not simply to cure them.

The condition was widespread among the Hebrews during and after their time in Egypt. Henry considers it likely that their harsh lives and work in Egypt made them especially vulnerable to illness, and he sees no reason to think this particular affliction was familiar among them earlier.

Yet some cases were evidently direct judgments from God.

Miriam, Gehazi and King Uzziah were struck with leprosy in connection with particular sins. It was therefore important to distinguish this affliction from an ordinary illness.

The priests were appointed to examine suspected cases.

Leprosy pictured the moral pollution of the soul by sin, which defiles the conscience and from which only Christ can cleanse us.

A priest could declare someone unclean, just as the law reveals knowledge of sin.

But the priest could not remove that uncleanness. Christ can truly take sin away.

Determining our spiritual condition is very important, yet difficult.

We are all aware of faults and stains in ourselves. The question is whether our spiritual condition is clean or unclean.

Just as marks helped the priest identify the physical affliction, spiritual signs can reveal whether a person remains trapped in bitterness and corruption.

The priest was to take time before pronouncing judgment.

This teaches ministers and ordinary believers not to condemn people hastily or judge before the proper time.

Some people's sins become apparent before judgment, while the sins of others—and likewise their good works—become visible only later.

Even when the person proved to be clean, the clothes still had to be washed because there had been reason for suspicion.

We all need the blood of Christ to wash us from our stains, even when they are not the severe marks of leprosy. Who among us can claim to be entirely free from sin?

Further signs of the affliction (verses 18–44)

The priest received instructions for cases where suspected leprosy appeared in an old sore.

Henry compares this to the spiritual danger faced by people who escape the world's corruption but later become entangled in it again.

He also considers cases where the disease appears in a burn (verse 24).

He sees in this a warning that strife and angry disputes can expose and intensify the corruption of the heart.

Human life is surrounded by many afflictions.

We face countless diseases, all of which entered the world because of sin.

When we enjoy health, strength and bodily comfort, we should use our bodies to glorify God.

Special attention was required when leprosy appeared on the head.

If the leprosy of sin corrupts a person's judgment, leading that person to accept false principles that support wicked behavior, the danger is especially grave.

Few people recover easily from deeply corrupt convictions.

Soundness in the faith helps protect the mind from that spiritual disease.

The person declared unclean (verses 45–46)

When a priest declared a person unclean, ordinary work stopped.

The person was separated from friends and family and deprived of many worldly comforts.

Such a person was to humble himself beneath God's mighty hand rather than insisting on a cleanness the priest had denied.

The spiritual lesson is that we should acknowledge the shame of our own sin.

With sorrowful hearts we must confess that both our hearts and lives have been unclean: through the corruption inherited from Adam and through our own acts of disobedience.

Because of these sins, we deserve to be excluded forever from fellowship with God unless his infinite mercy intervenes.

The leper had to warn others not to approach too closely.

The person was also required to live outside the camp. Later, in Canaan, this meant outside the town or village, apart from everyone except others suffering the same affliction.

Henry sees this as a picture of the purity that ought to characterize the Christian church.

Suspected contamination in clothing (verses 47–59)

Clothing suspected of leprosy was not to be burned immediately.

First it had to be examined.

If a persistent affected patch was found, the whole garment—or at least the affected part—was to be destroyed.

If the garment proved free of the affliction, it could be washed and used.

This, too, showed the serious evil of sin.

Sin stains not only the conscience but also a person's possessions and activities.

Those who use their clothes to display pride or indulge lust may see them spiritually stained.

But the robes of righteousness never decay or become moth-eaten.

Verses 1-17
The plague of leprosy was an uncleanness, rather than a disease. Christ is said to cleanse lepers, not to cure them. Common as the leprosy was among the Hebrews, during and after their residence in Egypt, we have no reason to believe that it was known among them before. Their distressed state and employment in that land must have rendered them liable to disease. But it was a plague often inflicted immediately by the hand of God. Miriam's leprosy, and Gehazi's, and king Uzziah's, were punishments of particular sins; no marvel there was care taken to distinguish it from a common distemper. The judgment of it was referred to the priests. And it was a figure of the moral pollutions of men's minds by sin, which is the leprosy of the soul, defiling to the conscience, and from which Christ alone can cleanse. The priest could only convict the leper, (by the law is the knowledge of sin,) but Christ can cure the sinner, he can take away sin. It is a work of great importance, but of great difficulty, to judge of our spiritual state. We all have cause to suspect ourselves, being conscious of sores and spots; but whether clean or unclean is the question. As there were certain marks by which to know it was leprosy, so there are marks of such as are in the gall of bitterness. The priest must take time in making his judgment. This teaches all, both ministers and people, not to be hasty in censures, nor to judge anything before the time. If some men's sins go before unto judgment, the sins of others follow after, and so do men's good works. If the person suspected were found to be clean, yet he must wash his clothes, because there had been ground for the suspicion. We have need to be washed in the blood of Christ from our spots, though not leprosy spots; for who can say, I am pure from sin?
[Lev.13.18-Lev.13.44]
Verses 18-44
The priest is told what judgment to make, if there were any appearance of a leprosy in old sores; and such is the danger of those who having escaped the pollutions of the world are again entangled therein. Or, in a burn by accident, ver. #(24). The burning of strife and contention often occasions the rising and breaking out of that corruption, which proves that men are unclean. Human life lies exposed to many grievances. With what troops of diseases are we beset on every side; and thy all entered by sin! If the constitution be healthy, and the body lively and easy, we are bound to glorify God with our bodies. Particular note was taken of the leprosy, if in the head. If the leprosy of sin has seized the head; if the judgment be corrupted, and wicked principles, which support wicked practices, are embraced, it is utter uncleanness, from which few are cleansed. Soundness in the faith keeps leprosy from the head.
[Lev.13.45-Lev.13.46]
Verses 45-46
When the priest had pronounced the leper unclean, it put a stop to his business in the world, cut him off from his friends and relations, and ruined all the comfort he could have in the world. He must humble himself under the mighty hand of God, not insisting upon his cleanness, when the priest had pronounced him unclean, but accepting the punishment. Thus must we take to ourselves the shame that belongs to us, and with broken hearts call ourselves "Unclean, unclean;" heart unclean, life unclean; unclean by original corruption, unclean by actual transgression; unclean, therefore deserving to be for ever shut out from communion with God, and all hope of happiness in him; unclean, therefore undone, if infinite mercy do not interpose. The leper must warn others to take heed of coming near him. He must then be shut out of the camp, and afterward, when they came to Canaan, be shut out of the city, town, or village where he lived, and dwell with none but those that were lepers like himself. This typified the purity which ought to be in the gospel church.
[Lev.13.47-Lev.13.59]
Verses 47-59
The garment suspected to be tainted with leprosy was not to be burned immediately. If, upon search, it was found that there was a leprous spot, it must be burned, or at least that part of it. If it proved to be free, it must be washed, and then might be used. This also sets forth the great evil there is in sin. It not only defiles the sinner's conscience, but it brings a stain upon all he has and all that he does. And those who make their clothes servants to their pride and lust, may see them thereby tainted with leprosy. But the robes of righteousness never fret, nor are moth-eaten.

Declaring a person cleansed (verses 1–9)

The priests could not heal leprosy.

But after the Lord removed the affliction, they were responsible for following the appointed ceremonies so that the person could again join the worship and fellowship of God's people.

The ceremonies illustrated the duties of people who truly repent and the responsibilities of ministers toward them.

Applied to the spiritual leprosy of sin, they teach us that when we withdraw from people who live disorderly lives, we must not treat them as enemies but warn them as brothers and sisters.

When God brings such people to repentance, we should welcome them back with tenderness, gladness and genuine love.

We must neither encourage people to remain in sin nor discourage those who repent.

When the priest found that a person had been healed, he formally declared that person clean through the prescribed ceremonies.

One bird was killed. A second was dipped in the blood of the first and then released.

Henry suggests this may picture Christ shedding his blood for sinners, then rising and ascending into heaven.

After being declared free from the affliction, the restored person still had to remove every trace of it.

Likewise, those who have the comfort of forgiveness should carefully turn away from their sins.

Everyone who possesses this hope seeks to become pure.

Offerings for a restored person (verses 10–32)

The restored person was to appear before the Lord with the appointed offerings.

When God enables us to return to public worship after sickness, distance or other obstacles, we should show gratitude by using that opportunity diligently.

Both we and our offerings must be brought before God by the Priest who cleanses us—our Lord Jesus Christ.

Alongside the ordinary rites of the guilt offering, blood and oil were placed on the person being cleansed.

Where Christ's blood is applied to bring justification, the oil of the Holy Spirit is also applied for sanctification.

These two blessings cannot be separated.

The law made gracious provision for the poor.

Poor people were as welcome at God's altar as the rich.

They could bring less costly sacrifices, but the essential ceremony was the same for everyone.

Their souls were equally precious, and the same Christ and gospel were needed by both.

Even the poorest had to bring one lamb.

No sinner could have been saved without the Lamb who was slain and redeemed us to God through his blood.

Suspected leprosy in a house (verses 33–53)

Leprosy in a house, like leprosy in a garment, is difficult for us to understand.

But where sin rules a household, it becomes a plague there just as surely as it does in an individual heart.

Heads of households should watch for the first signs of sin in their families and remove it, whatever form it takes.

If an affected section of a house was discovered, it had to be removed.

If the affliction remained, the entire building was to be pulled down.

It was better to lose a home than to continue living in one that remained contaminated.

The leprosy of sin can ruin both families and churches.

Sin is so deeply woven into our mortal bodies that those bodies must finally be brought down by death.

Concluding instruction on the law of leprosy (verses 54–57)

God is rich in mercy.

Because of his great love, even while we were dead in sins, he made us alive by his grace (Ephesians 2:4–5).

When he does this, we show the change by repenting and abandoning our former sins.

Let us pursue holiness.

Let us also show compassion toward other poor sufferers, sincerely desiring, seeking and praying for their cleansing.

The priests could not cleanse the lepers; but when the Lord removed the plague, various rules were to be observed in admitting them again to the ordinances of God, and the society of his people. They represent many duties and exercises of truly repenting sinners, and the duties of ministers respecting them. If we apply this to the spiritual leprosy of sin, it intimates that when we withdraw from those who walk disorderly, we must not count them as enemies, but admonish them as brethren. And also that when God by his grace has brought to repentance, they ought with tenderness and joy, and sincere affection, to be received again. Care should always be taken that sinners may not be encouraged, nor penitents discouraged. If it were found that the leprosy was healed, the priest must declare it with the particular solemnities here described. The two birds, one killed, and the other dipped in the blood of the bird that was killed, and then let loose, may signify Christ shedding his blood for sinners, and rising and ascending into heaven. The priest having pronounced the leper clean from the disease, he must make himself clean from all remains of it. Thus those who have comfort of the remission of their sins, must with care and caution cleanse themselves from sins; for every one that has this hope in him, will be concerned to purify himself.
[Lev.14.10-Lev.14.32]
Verses 10-32
The cleansed leper was to be presented to the Lord, with his offerings. When God has restored us to enjoy public worship again, after sickness, distance, or otherwise, we should testify our thanksgiving by our diligent use of the liberty. And both we and our offerings must be presented before the Lord, by the Priest that made us clean, even our Lord Jesus. Beside the usual rites of the trespass-offering, some of the blood, and some of the oil, was to be put upon him that was to be cleansed. Wherever the blood of Christ is applied for justification, the oil of the Spirit is applied for sanctification; these two cannot be separated. We have here the gracious provision the law made for poor lepers. The poor are as welcome to God's altar as the rich. But though a meaner sacrifice was accepted from the poor, yet the same ceremony was used for the rich; their souls are as precious, and Christ and his gospel are the same to both. Even for the poor one lamb was necessary. No sinner could be saved, had it not been for the Lamb that was slain, and hath redeemed us to God with his blood.
[Lev.14.33-Lev.14.53]
Verses 33-53
The leprosy in a house is unaccountable to us, as well as the leprosy in a garment; but now sin, where that reigns in a house, is a plague there, as it is in a heart. Masters of families should be aware, and afraid of the first appearance of sin in their families, and put it away, whatever it is. If the leprosy is got into the house, the infected part must be taken out. If it remain in the house, the whole must be pulled down. The owner had better be without a dwelling, than live in one that was infected. The leprosy of sin ruins families and churches. Thus sin is so interwoven with the human body, that it must be taken down by death.
[Lev.14.54-Lev.14.57]
Verses 54-57
When that God who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us by his grace, [Eph.2.4] Ep 2:4, [2Cor.2.5] 5, we shall manifest the change by repenting, and forsaking former sins. Let us follow after holiness, and let us compassionate other poor lepers, and desire, seek, and pray for their cleansing.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Laws concerning ceremonial uncleanness.

Ceremonial uncleanness and the need for purity

We do not need to speculate in great detail about these laws.

Rather, we have reason to give thanks that Christians are no longer obliged to undergo burdensome ceremonial purifications.

What truly defiles us is sin.

These regulations remind us that God sees everything, even things people never notice.

They point to the great duties of the gospel: faith and repentance.

They also illustrate its great privileges: Christ's blood applied to our souls for justification and his grace given for our sanctification.
classic_reading:
[Lev.15.1]
Chapter 15
Laws concerning ceremonial uncleanness.
--We need not be curious in explaining these laws; but have reason to be thankful that we need fear no defilement, except that of sin, nor need ceremonial and burdensome purifications. These laws remind us that God sees all things, even those which escape the notice of men. The great gospel duties of faith and repentance are here signified, and the great gospel privileges of the application of Christ's blood to our souls for our justification, and his grace for our sanctification.

The yearly Day of Atonement (verses 1–14)

Without detailing every ceremony of the great Day of Atonement, we should remember that its observance was to remain binding while that former religious order continued.

As long as we continue sinning, we continue to need atonement.

The duty of humbling and grieving over our sins remains until we reach the place where every tear—even tears of repentance—will be wiped away.

The apostle notes that the sacrifices themselves could never take sin away or cleanse the conscience completely.

Their repetition every year brought the memory of sin back again (Hebrews 10:1, 3).

That repeated offering revealed the weakness of the old sacrifices to achieve final atonement.

Only the offering of Christ's body once for all could do that.

His sacrifice does not need to be repeated.

The sacrifices and the scapegoat (verses 15–34)

The ceremonies pointed toward two great privileges of the gospel: forgiveness of sin and access to God.

Both come through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Look first at the removal of guilt.

Christ is both the Priest who makes atonement and the Sacrifice by which atonement is made.

He is everything necessary for our reconciliation to God.

The two goats pictured these aspects of his saving work.

The goat killed in sacrifice pointed to Christ's death for our sins.

The goat sent away pictured Christ rising again for our justification.

The priest symbolically placed Israel's sins on the head of the living goat and sent it away into an uninhabited wilderness.

Its departure represented the complete and free removal of the people's sins.

It bore away all their iniquities.

Likewise, Christ the Lamb of God takes away the world's sin by bearing it himself (John 1:29).

Look also at access to God.

The high priest's entry into the Most Holy Place pointed to Christ opening the way into heaven for us (Hebrews 9:7).

Israel's high priest came out again.

Our Lord Jesus lives forever, interceding continually and appearing in God's presence for us.

Finally, the ceremonies illustrated two great duties of the gospel: faith and repentance.

By faith, we place our hands upon the head of our offering, relying on Christ as the Lord our Righteousness and pleading his sacrifice as the only ground of pardon.

By repentance, we humble ourselves over sin.

That includes more than temporary fasting from bodily pleasures. It means sincere inward sorrow and a life of self-denial.

God is faithful and righteous to forgive people who confess their sins and to cleanse them from all unrighteousness.

Through Christ's atonement we receive rest for our souls and all the glorious freedom belonging to God's children.

If Christ's blood has not been truly applied to our souls, we cannot approach God with comfort or assurance of acceptance.

Receive that blood by faith and discover how completely it reconciles us to him.

Without entering into particulars of the sacrifices on the great day of atonement, we may notice that it was to be a statute for ever, till that dispensation be at an end. As long as we are continually sinning, we continually need the atonement. The law of afflicting our souls for sin, is a statue which will continue in force till we arrive where all tears, even those of repentance, will be wiped from our eyes. The apostle observes it as a proof that the sacrifices could not take away sin, and cleanse the conscience from it, that in them there was a remembrance made of sin every year, upon the day of atonement, [Heb.10.1] He 10:1, [Heb.10.3] 3. The repeating the sacrifices, showed there was in them but a feeble effort toward making atonement; this could be done only by offering up the body of Christ once for all; and that sacrifice needed not to be repeated. ( [Lev.16.15-Lev.16.34] Le 16:15-34)
[Lev.16.15-Lev.16.34]
Verses 15-34
Here are typified the two great gospel privileges, of the remission of sin, and access to God, both of which we owe to our Lord Jesus. See the expiation of guilt. Christ is both the Maker and the Matter of the atonement; for he is the Priest, the High Priest, that makes reconciliation for the sins of the people. And as Christ is the High Priest, so he is the Sacrifice with which atonement is made; for he is all in all in our reconciliation to God. Thus he was figured by the two goats. The slain goat was a type of Christ dying for our sins; the scape-goat a type of Christ rising again for our justification. The atonement is said to be completed by putting the sins of Israel upon the head of the goat, which was sent away into a wilderness, a land not inhabited; and the sending away of the goat represented the free and full remission of their sins. He shall bear upon him all their iniquities. Thus Christ, the Lamb of God, takes away the sin of the world, by taking it upon himself, [John.1.29] Joh 1:29. The entrance into heaven, which Christ made for us, was typified by the high priest's entrance into the most holy place. See [Heb.9.7] He 9:7. The high priest was to come out again; but our Lord Jesus ever lives, making intercession, and always appears in the presence of God for us. Here are typified the two great gospel duties of faith and repentance. By faith we put our hands upon the head of the offering; relying on Christ as the Lord our Righteousness, pleading his satisfaction, as that which alone is able to atone for our sins, and procure us a pardon. By repentance we afflict our souls; not only fasting for a time from the delights of the body, but inwardly sorrowing for sin, and living a life of self-denial, assuring ourselves, that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. By the atonement we obtain rest for our souls, and all the glorious liberties of the children of God. Sinner, get the blood of Christ effectually applied to thy soul, or else thou canst never look God in the face with any comfort or acceptance. Take this blood of Christ, apply it by faith, and see how it atones with God.

Sacrifices at the tabernacle (verses 1–9)

While the Israelites lived in the wilderness, every animal they killed from their herds was to be brought to the entrance of the tabernacle.

After being presented as an offering, its meat was returned to the owner to be eaten according to the regulations for fellowship offerings.

Once Israel entered Canaan, this requirement would apply only to animals offered in sacrifice.

Christians' spiritual sacrifices are no longer restricted to a particular location.

We have no earthly temple or altar that makes an offering acceptable.

The unity of the gospel is not founded on a single place, but on one heart and unity in the Spirit.

Christ is our Altar and the true Tabernacle.

God dwells among humanity in him.

Only through Christ can any offering be accepted by God.

To establish other mediators, altars or sacrifices supposed to make atonement would, in effect, be to establish other gods.

Yet God's willingness to accept the worship we offer in our homes is no excuse for neglecting the worship of his gathered people.

The prohibition concerning blood (verses 10–16)

The law forbidding Israel to eat blood is confirmed here.

But Henry explicitly says it was a ceremonial law and therefore no longer binds believers after Christ's coming.

The reality replaces its shadow.

Animal blood is no longer appointed as a ransom.

Only Christ's blood makes true and effective atonement.

The former reason for abstaining from blood has therefore ended, and it may now be used as ordinary nourishment.

But we must honor Christ's blood all the more.

It truly makes reconciliation with God.

We must never treat it as a common thing or regard it indifferently.

Here is a confirmation of the law against eating blood. They must eat no blood. But this law was ceremonial, and is now no longer in force; the coming of the substance does away the shadow. The blood is now allowed for the nourishment of our bodies; it is no longer appointed to make an atonement for the soul. Now the blood of Christ makes atonement really and effectually; to that, therefore, we must have regard, and not consider it as a common thing, or treat it with indifference.

modern_osis:
Original heading

Unlawful marriages and fleshly lusts.

Prohibitions against corrupt practices

This chapter forbids God's people to imitate the corrupt customs of the surrounding nations.

Its commands prohibit incest, degrading sexual acts and cruel idolatry.

The ruin of the Canaanites is given as a warning reinforcing these prohibitions.

God is giving moral commands here.

The most effective protection against gross sin is to keep closely and consistently to what God has appointed.

Only God's grace can preserve us from falling.

We should seek that grace through the means by which he has promised to give it.

God does not abandon people to their heart's sinful desires until they have first abandoned him and his service.

Unlawful marriages and fleshly lusts.
--Here is a law against all conformity to the corrupt usages of the heathen. Also laws against incest, against brutal lusts, and barbarous idolatries; and the enforcement of these laws from the ruin of the Canaanites. God here gives moral precepts. Close and constant adherence to God's ordinances is the most effectual preservative from gross sin. The grace of God only will secure us; that grace is to be expected only in the use of the means of grace. Nor does He ever leave any to their hearts' lusts, till they have left him and his services.

laws.

Holy conduct toward God and neighbor

This chapter includes a few ceremonial regulations, but most of its commands still bind us.

They explain and apply the Ten Commandments.

God calls Israel to holiness because Israel's God is holy (verse 2).

His people must separate themselves from worldly and sinful conduct and devote themselves completely to him.

This remains the law of Christ.

May the Lord bring our every thought into obedience to him!

Honor your parents (verse 3).

Children must respect and obey their parents from the heart.

They should value them, treat them respectfully, try to please them and ease their burdens.

Worship God alone (verse 4).

False gods deceive their worshipers and lead them toward misery.

The true God makes his people holy and happy.

Do not even turn your eyes toward idols, much less your hearts.

Leave part of the harvest for the poor (verse 9).

Acts of devotion must always be joined with acts of charity, according to our means.

We should not grasp at everything we have the right to claim, demanding the full extent of our rights in every situation.

Be honest in every dealing (verse 11).

Make sure that what you possess was obtained justly.

Dishonest gain cannot make a person truly or lastingly rich.

Revere God's holy name (verse 12).

Treat it seriously and respectfully.

Do not keep what belongs to someone else (verse 13).

This especially includes wages due to workers.

Protect those who cannot defend themselves (verse 14).

Guard their safety and reputation.

Do not harm anyone simply because that person cannot—or will not—retaliate.

Avoid even making a weaker brother or sister stumble.

Fear of God should restrain us from wrongdoing even when it cannot provoke human punishment.

Judge impartially (verse 15).

All those entrusted with authority must administer justice without favoritism.

Spreading malicious stories and sowing discord among neighbors is among the worst things a person can do.

Correct your neighbor in love (verse 17).

It is better to rebuke someone gently than to harbor hatred because that person has wronged you.

If we fail to correct our neighbor when we should, we become guilty ourselves; such silence is a form of hatred rather than love.

A loving friend can say, “I will do this person the kindness of pointing out the fault.”

Love your neighbor as yourself (verse 18).

Put aside malice and practice brotherly love.

We often forgive ourselves for wrongs we have committed, without loving ourselves any less.

We should show a similar readiness to forgive those around us.

We must often give up something we want for the good of another person.

Reject occult practices (verse 31).

Christians insult God when they seek predictions of the future, use charms or spells, or practice similar things.

Asking whether these activities are harmless shows serious ignorance of their spiritual danger.

Respect older people (verse 32).

Faith teaches us good manners and the obligation to honor those who deserve respect.

Care for foreigners (verse 33).

Foreigners, widows and orphans are objects of God's special concern.

Wronging them is dangerous and sinful.

God's grace is open to foreigners, and we should do what we can to commend his ways to them.

Use honest weights and measures (verse 35).

We must not choose only the commands we like.

Our aim should be to carry out the whole will of God.

The nearer our lives and dispositions come to his law, the more happiness we will find and bring to people around us, and the better we will adorn the gospel.

Chapter 19
laws.
--There are some ceremonial precepts in this chapter, but most of these precepts are binding on us, for they are explanations of the ten commandments. It is required that Israel be a holy people, because the God of Israel is a holy God, ver. #(2). To teach real separation from the world and the flesh, and entire devotedness to God. This is now the law of Christ; may the Lord bring every thought within us into obedience to it! Children are to be obedient to their parents, ver. #(3). The fear here required includes inward reverence and esteem, outward respect and obedience, care to please them and to make them easy. God only is to be worshipped, ver. #(4). Turn not from the true God to false ones, from the God who will make you holy and happy, to those that will deceive you, and make you for ever miserable. Turn not your eyes to them, much less your heart. They should leave the gleanings of their harvest and vintage for the poor, ver. #(9). Works of piety must be always attended with works of charity, according to our ability. We must not be covetous, griping, and greedy of every thing we can lay claim to, nor insist upon our right in all things. We are to be honest and true in all our dealings, ver. #(11). Whatever we have in the world, we must see that we get it honestly, for we cannot be truly rich, or long rich, with that which is not so. Reverence to the sacred name of God must be shown, ver. #(12). We must not detain what belongs to another, particularly the wages of the hireling, ver. #(13). We must be tender of the credit and safety of those that cannot help themselves, ver. #(14). Do no hurt to any, because they are unwilling or unable to avenge themselves. We ought to take heed of doing any thing which may occasion our weak brother to fall. The fear of God should keep us from doing wrong things, though they will not expose us to men's anger. Judges, and all in authority, are commanded to give judgment without partiality, ver. #(15). To be a tale-bearer, and to sow discord among neighbours, is as bad an office as a man can put himself into. We are to rebuke our neighbour in love, ver. #(17). Rather rebuke him than hate him, for an injury done to thyself. We incur guilt by not reproving; it is hating our brother. We should say, I will do him the kindness to tell him of his faults. We are to put off all malice, and to put on brotherly love, ver. #(18). We often wrong ourselves, but we soon forgive ourselves those wrongs, and they do not at all lessen our love to ourselves; in like manner we should love our neighbour. We must in many cases deny ourselves for the good of our neighbour. Ver. #(31): For Christians to have their fortunes told, to use spells and charms, or the like, is a sad affront to God. They must be grossly ignorant who ask, "What harm is there in these things?" Here is a charge to young people to show respect to the aged, ver. #(32). Religion teaches good manners, and obliges us to honour those to whom honour is due. A charge was given to the Israelites to be very tender of strangers, ver. #(33). Strangers, and the widows and fatherless, are God's particular care. It is at our peril, if we do them any wrong. Strangers shall be welcome to God's grace; we should do what we can to recommend religion to them. Justice in weights and measures is commanded, ver. #(35). We must make conscience of obeying God's precepts. We are not to pick and choose our duty, but must aim at standing complete in all the will of God. And the nearer our lives and tempers are to the precepts of God's law, the happier shall we be, and the happier shall we make all around us, and the better shall we adorn the gospel.

Child sacrifice and dishonoring parents (verses 1–9)

The cruelty of ancient idol worshipers who sacrificed their own children rightly shocks us.

But Henry warns that parents can also bring spiritual ruin on their children by teaching them evil, setting a wicked example and showing them habits of sin.

He regards this as an especially grievous wrong because it helps lead children toward eternal destruction.

What account will such parents give before God, and what will they say when they face their children at judgment?

Children, meanwhile, should remember the severe judgment pronounced on anyone who cursed a father or mother.

Christ confirmed the continuing moral force of this command.

These regulations repeat laws already given, this time with explicit penalties.

People ought to avoid evil because God's law declares it sinful.

But if they disregard that, they should at least fear the severe penalties for their own preservation.

Amid these solemn laws stands the command to consecrate ourselves and be holy.

The Lord himself makes his people holy and will accomplish his work, even when it is difficult.

His grace does not make our own effort unnecessary.

Rather, it powerfully encourages us to work out our salvation, because God is at work within us.

Repeated commands and the call to holiness (verses 10–27)

The laws in this passage repeat earlier instructions.

Such repetition was necessary: people need truth explained again and again.

How greatly we should praise God for showing us the evil of sin and the sure way to be delivered from it.

May his grace enable us to honor the teaching of God our Savior through everything we do.

May we refuse to participate in fruitless works of darkness and instead expose them.

[Lev.20.1-Lev.20.9]
Chapter 20
Chapter Outline
Law against sacrificing children to Moloch, Of children that curse their parents. | (1-9) |
Laws repeated, Holiness enjoined. | (10-27) |
Verses 1-9
Are we shocked at the unnatural cruelty of the ancient idolaters in sacrificing their children? We may justly be so. But are there not very many parents, who, by bad teaching and wicked examples, and by the mysteries of iniquity which they show their children, devote them to the service of Satan, and forward their everlasting ruin, in a manner even more to be lamented? What an account must such parents render to God, and what a meeting will they have with their children at the day of judgment! On the other hand, let children remember that he who cursed father or mother was surely put to death. This law Christ confirmed. Laws which were made before are repeated, and penalties annexed to them. If men will not avoid evil practices, because the law has made these practices sin, and it is right that we go on that principle, surely they should avoid them when the law has made them death, from a principle of self-preservation. In the midst of these laws comes in a general charge, Sanctify yourselves, and be ye holy. It is the Lord that sanctifies, and his work will be done, though it be difficult. Yet his grace is so far from doing away our endeavours, that it strongly encourages them. Work out your salvation, for it is God that worketh in you.
[Lev.20.10-Lev.20.27]
Verses 10-27
These verses repeat what had been said before, but it was needful there should be line upon line. What praises we owe to God that he has taught the evil of sin, and the sure way of deliverance from it! May we have grace to adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things; may we have no fellowship with unfruitful works of darkness, but reprove them.
